summary: Defines a MIB module for modeling the CAPWAP binding for IEEE 802.11 wireless. It is a basis for future work on managing that binding with SNMP. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It is a list of dials and gauges for the wifi-specific part of the system that runs wireless access points.

questions: how do you manage capwap wireless networks with snmp
what is a wlan profile in capwap
subtitle: Management framework for wireless access points controlled by a central system.

tldr.problem: Large networks need to manage hundreds of wireless access points and their configuration. Manual management is error-prone and does not scale, so a standard way to query and configure them via SNMP is needed.
tldr.mechanism: This MIB module defines a set of management objects for CAPWAP systems that use IEEE 802.11 wireless. It maps WLAN profiles (configuration bundles) to physical radios and provides tables to view and configure MAC mode, tunnel mode, and WLAN bindings.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now monitor and configure centrally managed wireless networks using standard SNMP tools, treating each wireless interface as a managed device.

today: RFC 5834 is Informational and provides the MIB foundation for CAPWAP 802.11 management. It remains the standard framework for managing centrally controlled wireless networks via SNMP, and RFC 5833 (the base CAPWAP MIB) was published alongside it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The CAPWAP protocol (defined in RFC 5415) enables a central Access Controller (AC) to manage a collection of Wireless Termination Points (WTPs)—the physical access points that broadcast WiFi. RFC 5416 defines how CAPWAP works with IEEE 802.11 wireless technology.

This MIB module provides the management framework for CAPWAP systems using 802.11 binding. It allows network operators to query and configure wireless networks through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), the standard tool for managing network devices. The module defines two main data structures: one for configuring WLAN profiles on the central controller, and another for binding those profiles to physical radios.
sections.eli5: When you have a bunch of WiFi access points spread across a building, you need a way to manage them all from one place. SNMP is the standard tool for that, and this MIB module is the instruction manual.

sections.title: Key Concepts: CAPWAP Architecture
sections.content:
In a CAPWAP-based wireless network, the system is split into two main parts: the Access Controller (AC) and Wireless Termination Points (WTPs).

The Access Controller is the central device that manages policy, authentication, and configuration. It communicates with WTPs using the CAPWAP protocol, which can run over a secure DTLS channel to protect configuration data.

A Wireless Termination Point is a physical access point with a radio antenna and wireless radio card. It receives configuration from the AC and transmits and receives user traffic. A single physical WTP can host multiple WLANs, each identified by a Basic Service Set Identifier (BSSID).

The CAPWAP protocol supports two modes of operation: Split MAC (where the AC handles most wireless frame processing) and Local MAC (where the WTP handles data frames locally). This MIB module allows operators to configure which mode to use for each WLAN.
sections.eli5: Imagine a hotel with one front desk (the AC) and many door locks (the WTPs). The front desk tells each lock what rules to follow. This framework lets you check and change those rules from a single dashboard.

sections.title: Managing WLAN Profiles
sections.content:
The module's core feature is the capwapDot11WlanTable, which stores WLAN profiles on the Access Controller. Each profile is a bundle of configuration for a wireless network: the WLAN's MAC mode (Split or Local), and its tunnel mode (how data frames are forwarded).

The operator creates a WLAN profile by adding a row to the table, specifying which mode to use. When the profile is created, the AC automatically generates a WLAN Profile Interface and assigns it an interface index (ifIndex). This index acts like a handle that links the profile to the IEEE 802.11 MIB module, allowing the operator to reuse existing 802.11 configuration tables to set authentication methods, RTS thresholds, and other radio parameters.

A single AC can host more than 16 WLAN profiles, but each physical radio can bind a maximum of 16 distinct WLANs at a time (identified by WLAN IDs 1 through 16). This allows a single access point to broadcast multiple SSIDs, each with different security or bandwidth settings.
sections.eli5: A WLAN profile is like a template you create once that says 'split the work between the access point and central controller' or 'let the access point handle it all'. You give it a number and then attach it to a real radio.

sections.title: Binding Profiles to Radios and Data Forwarding
sections.content:
The second key table is the capwapDot11WlanBindTable. This table records which WLAN profiles are active on which physical radios. When an operator binds a profile to a radio, the AC automatically creates a WLAN BSS Interface (Basic Service Set Interface) for data forwarding.

Each binding row contains: the interface index of the WTP Virtual Radio Interface (representing the physical radio on the WTP), the WLAN profile ID, the assigned WLAN ID (1 to 16), and the interface index of the resulting WLAN BSS Interface (used for data traffic). The AC ensures that WLAN IDs are unique within each radio to avoid collisions.

The physical address (MAC address) of a WLAN BSS Interface is the BSSID. Although vendors can assign BSSIDs arbitrarily, the RFC recommends a simple scheme: base BSSID address plus the WLAN ID. This allows the WTP to quickly derive the BSSID from the profile without needing a lookup table.
sections.eli5: When you plug a template into a radio, the system automatically assigns it a number (the WLAN ID) and creates a data channel with its own MAC address. Multiple templates can be plugged into the same radio, giving you multiple networks on one access point.

sections.title: Integration with IEEE 802.11 and System Administration
sections.content:
The CAPWAP 802.11 MIB module is not a replacement for the IEEE 802.11 MIB module [IEEE.802-11.2007]—instead, it reuses it. The ifIndex values created for WLAN profiles and WLAN BSS interfaces serve as anchors that link into the IEEE 802.11 MIB tables (such as dot11OperationTable for configuring RTS thresholds, or dot11AuthenticationAlgorithmsTable for setting security methods).

This design allows operators to manage both the CAPWAP-specific parts (profile configuration, binding) and the radio-specific parts (802.11 parameters) from a single management system. The MIB module also integrates with the SNMPv2-MIB for system identity, and with the Interfaces Group (IF-MIB) for generic interface management.

The RFC also specifies an IANA-assigned ifType value for WLAN Profile Interfaces (type 252) and WLAN BSS Interfaces (type 253), making them recognizable to all SNMP tools. The AC must preserve these interface indices across reboot so that configuration persists and management systems can reliably track resources.
sections.eli5: The management system talks to both the central controller (using this MIB) and to the standard WiFi library (using the 802.11 MIB). They use the same interface numbers as the meeting point, so changes in one place automatically apply to the other.
